23Math · Optimization

Steepest descent → learning rate → mini-batches → Adam: the math of every training step.

ⓘ Notes
Proves that the negative gradient is the steepest descent direction, the learning-rate convergence condition, that mini-batch gradients are unbiased with variance falling as 1/B, and where Adam’s bias correction comes from.

Why it’s designed this way: The answers to “it diverged”, “too noisy” and “what learning rate?” are all here.

Stop 23 of 24 📍 App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Math · Optimization
On this page:

🧒 In plain words first

Training a model is like walking down a hill blindfolded: you cannot see the bottom, but your feet can feel which way slopes down most steeply, so you take a small step that way, feel again, and step again. Here “how high you are” is how wrong the model is (the loss).

This stop explains why a few downhill tricks work: why you head the steepest way down; how big each step should be (the learning rate); why you can estimate the slope from a small handful of examples (mini-batches); and how remembering your last few steps makes the walk steadier (momentum and Adam).

② Diagram

Go deeper (the full explanation)

The Loss function is a landscape with hundreds of millions of dimensions. Gradient descent takes a small step along the steepest way down; the Learning rate & convergence sets the step size; Stochastic gradient (mini-batch) estimates the slope from a small batch; Momentum & Adam smooths that noisy slope. This stop proves why each of these works.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

Standing on a hillside, you could step in any direction. The “slope” (the gradient) tells you how fast the height changes in each direction. It points the steepest way uphill, so to go down you walk the opposite way.

This card proves that, among all small steps of the same length, the opposite way makes the height drop fastest. The proof uses a small tool (the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality): multiplying two lists of numbers position by position and adding up never gives something bigger than the two lists’ “lengths” multiplied together.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

To be more exact…“Drops fastest” holds only right around the current point, for very small steps (it is about the rate of change). Real landscapes curve: with a big step the steepest direction need not stay the best one, which is why the step must be small enough to be sure the loss goes down. Where the slope is 0 (at the bottom of a valley, say) there is no downhill direction to take.

θ ← θ−η ∇L(θ)\theta\ \leftarrow\ \theta-\eta\,\nabla L(\theta)θ ← θ−η∇L(θ)

🔤 What the symbols mean

  • Say: “theta”all of the model’s “knobs” (parameters) together
  • Say: “becomes”Work out the right side, then store it on the left, replacing the old value, like rubbing out a scoreboard and writing the new score.
  • Say: “eta”the learning rate: how big each step is
  • Say: no word: side by side means timesTwo things written right next to each other, with no sign between them, are multiplied: a number right before a letter means that number times it; two brackets side by side are multiplied.
  • Say: “nabla” or “del”: the gradientThe “gradient”: how fast things change in each input direction, put in a list. It points the steepest way uphill; training takes a small step the opposite way so the loss goes down.
  • Say: “L”the loss: how wrong the model is (the “height of the hill”)
  • Say: “… of …”What comes out when you put the thing in brackets into the “machine” (function) named in front. Like a vending machine: put something in, get something out.

  • Say: “is not equal to”The two sides are not the same.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

The learning rate is “how big each step is”. Too small, and you crawl like an ant, never arriving before dark; too big, and one step leaps across the valley to a higher spot on the other side, then the leaps get bigger and bigger. That is called diverging.

In the simplest “bowl-shaped” valley you can work out every step exactly: below a certain limit, the steps always reach the bottom of the bowl; at or above it, they bounce back and forth forever, or even fly further and further away. The steeper the bowl, the smaller the limit.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

To be more exact…The limit is exact only for a perfect bowl (a quadratic function). With many directions, the limit is set by the steepest one; real loss landscapes are not perfect bowls, so the limit here is only a guide.

The simplest landscape makes it clear: f(x)=a2x2f(x)=\tfrac{a}{2}x^2f(x)=2a​x2 with a>0a>0a>0, minimum at x=0x=0x=0, f′(x)=axf'(x)=axf′(x)=ax.

📝 Gradient descent converges iff 0<η<2/a0<\eta<2/a0<η<2/a

    • Say: “a”how steep the bowl is (a number above 0)

Q.E.D. ∎

  • 0<η<1/a0<\eta<1/a0<η<1/a: shrinks the same side every step, a smooth approach.
  • η=1/a\eta=1/aη=1/a: lands on the minimum in one step.
  • 1/a<η<2/a1/a<\eta<2/a1/a<η<2/a: bounces from side to side but shrinks, still converges.
  • η≥2/a\eta\ge 2/aη≥2/a: bounces forever (equality) or further and further out (divergence).

Explained above:

⚠️ Mix-up

🧒 In plain words first

Walking downhill, the gradient is the slope under your feet: which way is lower and how steep, re-checked at every step. The learning rate is the stride you choose. Steep slope and long stride means one big step.

In one line: the gradient is computed at every step: it says which way is uphill and how steep; the learning rate is a number people set in advance: how big a stride to take downhill. One step = learning rate × gradient, in the opposite direction.

CompareGradient gLearning rate η
Where fromcomputed from the current parameters and this batch (backpropagation)a hyperparameter people choose; it may follow a schedule over time
What it isa list of numbers, one per parameterusually one number (e.g. 0.001)
Controlsdirection and steepnessstride length
Changes every step?yes, it changes whenever the position doesnot by itself, unless you set a schedule

Example (made-up numbers):The update θ ← θ − η·g (θ is a parameter, ← means “replace with”). If one parameter’s gradient is g = 4 and the learning rate is η = 0.1, this step lowers it by 0.1 × 4 = 0.4. Double the gradient and the step doubles; too large a learning rate jumps right over the valley.

🧠 Remember: the gradient is the arrow on the map (re-read at every step); the learning rate is your stride (your choice).

👉 See also:

🧪 LabIllustrative

🧪 Learning rate and convergence: 12 steps on f(x) = x²

🧒 In plain words first

Drag the slider to change η (say “eta”: how big each step is) and watch a point take 12 steps on the bowl-shaped curve f(x) = x². x₀ is the starting point, and a says how steep the bowl is (here a = 2). See which step sizes walk calmly to the bottom and which start bouncing wildly.

ⓘ The landscape is f(x) = x² (a = 2), starting at x₀ = 3; every step is computed exactly.

Why it’s built this way:
  • The proof says the threshold is 2/a = 1; drag past 1 and watch convergence turn into divergence.
👀 Try this:
  • η = 0.5: one step to the bottom (η = 1/a).
  • η = 0.8: bounces left and right but closes in.
  • η = 1: bounces between 3 and −3 forever; from η = 1.05 it flies off.
③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

There might be millions of practice examples. Working through all of them before every single step would be far too slow. Instead, each step picks a small random handful (say 32) and estimates the slope from those.

It is like tasting one spoonful of soup to tell if it is salty: you do not have to drink the whole pot. A spoonful can be a little off, but on average it is not tilted either way; the more you pick, the closer it gets: picking 4 times as many halves the error.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

To be more exact…“Not tilted on average” means the estimate’s expected value equals the true slope exactly (it is unbiased). The “error” is the estimate’s standard deviation, which shrinks with the square root of the number picked. The analysis assumes each pick is uniform and with replacement; picking without replacement makes the error a little smaller still.

The full loss is the average over all NNN examples, L=1N∑i=1NℓiL=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}\ell_iL=N1​∑i=1N​ℓi​, and its exact gradient is too expensive. Mini-batches & epochs instead draws BBB examples at random each step (analysed here as uniform sampling with replacement) and uses their average gradient:

g^=1B∑b=1B∇ℓib,ib uniform on {1,…,N}\hat g=\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^{B}\nabla\ell_{i_b},\qquad i_b\ \text{uniform on}\ \{1,\dots,N\}g^​=B1​b=1∑B​∇ℓib​​,ib​ uniform on {1,…,N}
g^=1B∑b=1B∇ℓibib uniform on {1,…,N}\begin{gathered}\begin{aligned}\hat g&=\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^{B}\nabla\ell_{i_b}\end{aligned}\\i_b\ \text{uniform on}\ \{1,\dots,N\}\end{gathered}g^​​=B1​b=1∑B​∇ℓib​​​ib​ uniform on {1,…,N}​
g^=1B∑b=1B∇ℓibib uniform on {1,…,N}\begin{gathered}\begin{aligned}&\hat g\\&\quad =\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^{B}\nabla\ell_{i_b}\end{aligned}\\i_b\ \text{uniform on}\ \{1,\dots,N\}\end{gathered}​g^​=B1​b=1∑B​∇ℓib​​​ib​ uniform on {1,…,N}​

🔤 What the symbols mean

  • Say: “hat”A little hat on a letter usually means the guessed or predicted value, to tell it apart from the real one.
  • Say: “g”the slope estimated from this handful (the hat means “an estimate”)
  • Say: “over” (the fraction bar)The top is divided by the bottom. ½ is 1 divided by 2, which is one half.
  • Say: no word: side by side means timesTwo things written right next to each other, with no sign between them, are multiplied: a number right before a letter means that number times it; two brackets side by side are multiplied.
  • Say: “B”how many examples are picked each time (the batch size)
  • Say: “sigma” (sum)“Add up a whole list.” Below: where to start; above: where to stop. With only a letter below, add over every possible value of it.
  • Say: “b”a label: which pick in this handful
  • Say: “nabla” or “del”: the gradientThe “gradient”: how fast things change in each input direction, put in a list. It points the steepest way uphill; training takes a small step the opposite way so the loss goes down.
  • Say: “script l”the loss on one example
  • Say: “sub” (the small lowered mark)A small lowered mark is a number or a label that tells apart several things of the same kind: label 1 and label 2 are the 1st one and the 2nd one.
  • Say: “i”a label: which example
  • Say: “uniform on”pick one of these labels at random, each equally likely
  • Say: “dot dot dot”“Many more in between, following the same pattern; we don’t write them all out.”

⚠️ Mix-up

🧒 In plain words first

A workbook has 1000 questions. Each time you do 32, check them and adjust once: that pile is a batch and the adjustment a step; finishing the whole book once is an epoch. So one epoch takes 32 steps (the last pile has only 8).

In one line: a batch is a small pile of examples used for one gradient; a step is one parameter update made with one batch; an epoch is one full pass over the whole training set. Steps per epoch = examples ÷ batch size (rounded up if it does not divide).

📦 Batch

  • What: a small pile of examples; how many is the batch size B
  • Like: the stack of homework a teacher marks in one go
  • Example: B = 32: take 32 examples each time

👣 Step

  • What: compute one average gradient, update the parameters once
  • Like: one round of feedback after a stack is marked
  • Example: 1 batch → 1 step (ignoring gradient accumulation)

🔁 Epoch

  • What: every training example used once
  • Like: working through the whole workbook once
  • Example: 1000 examples, B = 32: one epoch = ⌈1000 ÷ 32⌉ = 32 steps (the last batch has only 8)
  • ⌈ ⌉ means “round up”: 31.25 becomes 32. Some programs drop the last, short batch, and then one epoch is 31 steps.
  • A common practice: shuffle the data at the start of each epoch, then cut it into batches, so each example is used exactly once per epoch, in different groups every time.
  • “Gradient accumulation” is the exception: gradients from several batches are added up before one update, so several batches make one step.
  • Large models see so much data that they often make only about one pass, so people talk about “how many steps / tokens”, not epochs.

🧠 Remember: a batch is a pile, a step is one update, an epoch is the whole book once. Total steps = steps per epoch × epochs.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

The slope estimated from a small handful “wobbles”. Momentum works like a ball rolling downhill: it remembers which way it was rolling, so the odd little bump cancels out, while a slope that keeps going the same way makes it roll faster and faster.

Adam goes further and gives every “knob” (parameter) its own step size: it remembers how big each knob’s recent slopes usually are and adjusts the step by that size, so a knob with a huge slope does not leap too far at once, and one with a tiny slope does not barely move. At the start these “memories” begin at 0 and come out too small, so they are scaled back up by a correction factor.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

To be more exact…Adam’s step is roughly independent of the slope’s “scale”, but it is not exactly fixed. The correction factor makes the memories not too small on average, under the assumption that the slopes’ average does not change over time.

Momentum accumulates past gradients, so noisy directions cancel and consistent ones speed up:

Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014) tracks a moving average m of the gradient and v of its square, and applies a “bias correction”:
